Omics data break the habits acquired in the rest of this course. There are more variables than samples - five thousand genes measured in a hundred and thirty-eight tissue pieces - so every analysis is a multiple-comparison problem before it is anything else; the samples are not independent, because two of them come from the same patient; and the observations themselves are related by evolution, so two protein sequences in a training set can be the same protein read in two species. This unit works through the complete path on two frozen datasets the group uses: 621 reviewed UniProt sequences from six protein families, where a random train/test split quietly hides homology leakage, and the periodontitis expression matrix, from quality control through a paired differential-expression model and false-discovery-rate control to over-representation and gene-set enrichment analysis implemented from their definitions, finishing with the four ways an omics analysis most often goes wrong.

Resumen en español

Esta unidad recorre el análisis de datos de secuencias y de expresión génica. Primero se manipulan 621 secuencias reales de proteínas revisadas de UniProt, repartidas en seis familias (globinas, proteasas de serina S1, lisozima C, anhidrasas carbónicas alfa, quinasas AGC y citocromos P450), con Biopython: lectura de FASTA, composición de aminoácidos, propiedades fisicoquímicas y vectores de k-meros. Un clasificador de familias alcanza 0,947 de exactitud con partición aleatoria y 0,879 cuando los grupos de secuencias homólogas se mantienen enteros en un solo pliegue; el diagnóstico decisivo es que con partición aleatoria el 22 % de las secuencias de prueba tiene un pariente casi idéntico en el conjunto de entrenamiento, y con partición por grupos ese porcentaje baja a cero. Luego se analiza la matriz de expresión congelada del estudio de periodontitis (5.000 genes x 138 muestras, 69 pares enfermo/sano del mismo paciente): control de calidad, PCA, un modelo lineal pareado ajustado con statsmodels que reproduce exactamente la prueba t pareada, control de la tasa de falsos descubrimientos con Benjamini-Hochberg (3.766 genes con FDR < 0,05 en el análisis pareado frente a 3.420 sin parear) y umbrales de tamaño de efecto. Se construyen los gráficos habituales (volcán, MA, mapa de calor) y se interpretan los resultados con análisis de sobre-representación hipergeométrico y con un GSEA por permutaciones programado desde su definición. La unidad termina con los errores característicos de la ómica: p mucho mayor que n, esquemas de permutación que ignoran el diseño pareado, doble uso de los datos, la maldición del ganador y los límites de una sola cohorte sin covariables demográficas.

Learning objectives

  • Handle sequence data programmatically with Biopython: parsing, composition, physico-chemical descriptors and k-mer features, and build a protein-family classifier evaluated with a group split.
  • Normalise and explore an expression matrix (distributions, library-size proxies, PCA, structure that is not biology) and run a differential-expression analysis with correct multiple-testing control.
  • Perform and interpret over-representation and gene-set enrichment analysis, and present results (volcano, MA, heatmap, enrichment plots) without the usual misreadings.
  • Recognise the specific pitfalls of omics: p much greater than n, homology and batch structure, double dipping, circular enrichment, the winner's curse and the limits of a single cohort.

How to read this notebook

Read it linearly with the code running; every number in the prose is printed by a cell of this notebook. In Google Colab run !pip install biopython statsmodels once before the setup cell; the analysis uses Biopython[1], NumPy[30], SciPy[31], scikit-learn[28], statsmodels[29] and matplotlib[32]. This is an extended unit: students whose project does not involve expression data can read sections 1-3 and stop. It builds on Unit 8 (multiple comparisons), Unit 9 (linear models), Unit 12 (group splits and leakage) and Unit 13 (PCA). The whole notebook runs in about three minutes.

1. Two kinds of omics data

Domain context

A gene is a stretch of DNA transcribed into messenger RNA and usually translated into a protein, a chain of twenty kinds of amino acid written as letters (M for methionine, W for tryptophan, and so on). A protein family groups proteins that descend from a common ancestor and share a fold and a function; orthologues are the same protein in different species (human and mouse myoglobin) and paralogues are copies within one genome that diverged after duplication (haemoglobin alpha and beta). Both are homologues, and both make two rows of a sequence table statistically dependent. UniProt[33] is the reference protein knowledgebase; its reviewed (Swiss-Prot) section is manually curated and carries a family annotation, which is where the labels used here come from. The transcriptome is the set of mRNA abundances in a tissue sample: a microarray measures them as fluorescence intensities on probes, and RNA sequencing measures them as read counts. The expression data used here come from a microarray study of periodontitis, a chronic inflammatory disease of the tissues around the teeth, in which each patient contributed one diseased gingival site and one clinically healthy site - a paired design. The values are log2 RMA intensities[17], so a difference of 1 means a two-fold change in abundance. A gene set is a curated list of genes sharing an annotation - a KEGG pathway[20] or a Gene Ontology biological process[18][19] - and enrichment asks whether the genes a study highlights fall into such a list more often than chance.

Both datasets are frozen with the course. protein_families.csv and protein_families.fasta hold 621 reviewed UniProt sequences in six families - globin (118), peptidase S1 (118), lysozyme C (118), alpha-carbonic anhydrase (108), AGC protein kinase (99) and cytochrome P450 (60) - with the accession, organism, length, sequence and UniProt's own family string. geo_periodontitis_expr.csv is the slice of GEO series GSE16134[13] studied by the group's collaborators[14][15][16]: the 5,000 most variable genes across 138 samples, 69 patients x (one diseased site + one healthy site). That series carries no demographic covariates at all - no age, no sex, no smoking status - which is itself a lesson about public data and is the reason the structure modelled below is the patient rather than a batch.

from collections import Counter
KMERS = ["".join(p) for p in product(AAs, repeat=2)]
KIDX = {k: i for i, k in enumerate(KMERS)}
def kmer_features(s, k=2):
    '''Relative frequency of each of the 400 dipeptides; letters outside the standard 20 are ignored.'''
    v = np.zeros(len(KMERS))
    for i in range(len(s) - k + 1):
        j = KIDX.get(s[i:i + k])
        if j is not None:
            v[j] += 1
    return v / max(1, len(s) - k + 1)

X = normalize(np.array([kmer_features(s) for s in fam["sequence"]]))     # L2-normalised dipeptide profiles
y = fam["family"].to_numpy(dtype=object)                                  # pandas 3: dtype=object for sklearn

# A similarity matrix over 3-mer profiles, used both as an identity proxy and to define homology groups.
vocab, counts = {}, []
for s in fam["sequence"]:
    c = Counter(s[i:i + 3] for i in range(len(s) - 2)); counts.append(c)
    for k_ in c:
        vocab.setdefault(k_, len(vocab))
M = np.zeros((len(fam), len(vocab)), dtype=np.float32)
for i, c in enumerate(counts):
    for k_, v in c.items():
        M[i, vocab[k_]] = v
Mn = normalize(M)
SIM = Mn @ Mn.T                                   # cosine similarity of 3-mer profiles, 0 to 1
np.fill_diagonal(SIM, 1.0)
dist = np.clip(1 - SIM, 0, None)
Zlink = linkage(squareform(dist, checks=False), method="average")
groups = fcluster(Zlink, t=0.5, criterion="distance")      # homology groups: average-linkage at cosine distance 0.5
print("3-mer profile similarity: mean over all pairs %.3f" % SIM[np.triu_indices(len(fam), 1)].mean())
ly = fam.index[fam["protein_name"].str.startswith("Lysozyme C ")].to_numpy()
print("mean similarity among the %d 'Lysozyme C' entries: %.3f" % (len(ly), SIM[np.ix_(ly, ly)][np.triu_indices(len(ly), 1)].mean()))
print("homology groups at cosine distance 0.5: %d groups, largest %d members, %d singletons"
      % (len(set(groups)), np.bincount(groups).max(), int((np.bincount(groups)[1:] == 1).sum())))

3-mer profile similarity: mean over all pairs 0.070
mean similarity among the 46 'Lysozyme C' entries: 0.369

models = {"1-NN (cosine)": KNeighborsClassifier(1, metric="cosine"),
          "logistic regression": LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000, C=5.0),
          "random forest": RandomForestClassifier(300, random_state=0, n_jobs=-1)}
name_groups = fam["protein_name"].to_numpy(dtype=object)
res_split = {}
for label, model in models.items():
    rnd = cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)).mean()
    g_name = cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=GroupKFold(5), groups=name_groups).mean()
    g_hom = cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=GroupKFold(5), groups=groups).mean()
    res_split[label] = (rnd, g_name, g_hom)
    print("%-20s random 5-fold %.3f | grouped by protein name %.3f | grouped by homology cluster %.3f"
          % (label, rnd, g_name, g_hom))
print("majority-class baseline %.3f" % fam["family"].value_counts(normalize=True).max())
print("\nNote: the grouping variable cannot be the family itself - a fold missing a whole class cannot be scored.")

2. Why a random split flatters a sequence classifier

Three models, three protocols, one data set. Every model loses accuracy when homologous sequences are kept together, and the loss depends on how much the model relies on recognising individual sequences: the nearest-neighbour classifier falls from 0.947 to 0.879, while logistic regression on the same features falls only from 0.995 to 0.982. That asymmetry is itself the lesson. A model that generalises over composition barely notices the change; a model whose prediction is "find the most similar training sequence" - the machine-learning version of a BLAST search - loses most of what a random split gave it.

The accuracy gap understates the problem, because this six-family task is easy: the families differ in length by a factor of four (mean 145 residues for lysozyme C against 634 for the AGC kinases) and in composition by a lot (6.1 % cysteine in lysozyme C against 2.0 % elsewhere). The honest diagnostic is not the accuracy drop but the composition of the test set: how similar is each test sequence to the nearest sequence the model was allowed to train on? The next cell measures exactly that, under both protocols.

def max_similarity_to_training(cv, groups=None):
    '''For every test sequence, its similarity to the most similar training sequence.'''
    out = []
    splits = cv.split(X, y, groups) if groups is not None else cv.split(X, y)
    for train_idx, test_idx in splits:
        out.append(SIM[np.ix_(test_idx, train_idx)].max(axis=1))
    return np.concatenate(out)

ms_random = max_similarity_to_training(StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0))
ms_group = max_similarity_to_training(GroupKFold(5), groups=groups)
for label, v in [("random split", ms_random), ("homology-group split", ms_group)]:
    print("%-22s median %.3f | at least 0.9 similar: %4.1f %% | at least 0.7: %4.1f %%"
          % (label, np.median(v), 100 * (v >= 0.9).mean(), 100 * (v >= 0.7).mean()))

rng_lc = np.random.default_rng(0)
print("\ntraining-set size experiment (1-NN cosine, mean of 20 repeats):")
curve = []
for n_train in (30, 60, 120, 240):
    acc_r, acc_g = [], []
    for _ in range(20):
        idx = rng_lc.permutation(len(X))[:n_train]
        test = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(len(X)), idx)
        acc_r.append((KNeighborsClassifier(1, metric="cosine").fit(X[idx], y[idx]).predict(X[test]) == y[test]).mean())
        keep = []
        for c in rng_lc.permutation(np.unique(groups)):
            keep += list(np.where(groups == c)[0])
            if len(keep) >= n_train:
                break
        keep = np.array(keep[:n_train])
        if len(set(y[keep])) < fam["family"].nunique():
            continue
        held = np.array([i for i in range(len(X)) if groups[i] not in set(groups[keep])])
        acc_g.append((KNeighborsClassifier(1, metric="cosine").fit(X[keep], y[keep]).predict(X[held]) == y[held]).mean())
    curve.append((n_train, np.mean(acc_r), np.mean(acc_g)))
    print("   n_train = %3d : random %.3f | homology-disjoint %.3f | gap %.3f"
          % (n_train, np.mean(acc_r), np.mean(acc_g), np.mean(acc_r) - np.mean(acc_g)))

random split           median 0.585 | at least 0.9 similar: 22.4 % | at least 0.7: 40.6 %
homology-group split   median 0.318 | at least 0.9 similar:  0.0 % | at least 0.7:  0.0 %

training-set size experiment (1-NN cosine, mean of 20 repeats):
   n_train =  30 : random 0.700 | homology-disjoint 0.571 | gap 0.129
   n_train =  60 : random 0.786 | homology-disjoint 0.686 | gap 0.100
   n_train = 120 : random 0.862 | homology-disjoint 0.760 | gap 0.102
   n_train = 240 : random 0.909 | homology-disjoint 0.827 | gap 0.082

Figure 1. Left: the first two principal components of the L2-normalised dipeptide profiles; the six families occupy distinguishable regions, which is why every classifier scores well. Centre: the diagnostic that matters. Under a random split the median test sequence has a nearest training relative at similarity 0.585, 22 % of test sequences have one above 0.9 and 41 % above 0.7; under the homology-group split the median falls to 0.318 and no test sequence has a relative above 0.7 - the orthologues have been removed from the training set, which is what a group split is for. Right: the accuracy consequence, large for the nearest-neighbour model (0.947 to 0.879) and small for logistic regression and the random forest.

The practical protocol follows directly, and it is the standard one in protein machine learning[34][35]: cluster the sequences at an identity threshold (CD-HIT, MMseqs2, or the pre-computed UniRef50/UniRef90 clusters), then make those clusters the groups of a group-aware cross-validator, and report the grouped number as the performance of the method. Here the clustering is done inside the notebook from 3-mer profile similarity - 345 groups from 621 sequences, the largest with 33 members, 256 of them singletons - which is a proxy for sequence identity, not a substitute for a real alignment-based clustering.

Two further points are worth stating because students meet them immediately. First, the grouping variable cannot be the class label: a fold that contains no globin at all cannot be scored on globins. Grouping by protein name (411 groups, accuracy 0.881 for the nearest-neighbour model) and grouping by homology cluster (345 groups, 0.879) agree closely here, so either is defensible, but both must be reported for what they are. Second, the penalty of the honest protocol grows as the training set shrinks: with 240 training sequences the nearest-neighbour gap is 0.082, with 30 it is 0.129 - and 30 sequences is the realistic size of a thesis project's curated set.

Exercise 1

Re-cut the homology groups at cosine distance 0.3 and at 0.7 (change t= in the fcluster call) and repeat the three-model comparison. How do the number of groups and the grouped accuracy move, and which cut would you defend to a reviewer who asks "at what identity did you cluster"? Then repeat the comparison using only the 20 amino-acid composition features instead of the 400 dipeptides: does the simpler feature set suffer more or less from homology leakage, and why?

Figure 2. Left: per-sample distributions of the first 24 arrays; RMA has already quantile- normalised them, so medians and quartiles coincide and no further normalisation is applied. Centre: the pooled histogram is bimodal, the lower mode being genes close to background. Right: the library-size proxy varies by only 2.2 % (coefficient of variation) and the diseased (red) and healthy (blue) samples are interleaved, so there is no depth confounding of the kind that count-based RNA-seq data would require normalising away.

This is also where the choice of statistical machinery is made. These are continuous, already normalised log2 intensities, not counts. The negative-binomial machinery of DESeq2[2] and its Python port PyDESeq2[3] models integer counts with a mean-variance relationship that microarray intensities do not have; applying it here would be a category error. Count-specific pipelines and their best practices[27] therefore do not transfer directly. The correct tool is a linear model per gene with moderated variance - the limma approach[4][5] - and the paired design enters as a patient term. We fit the linear model with statsmodels and implement the multiple-testing control ourselves, which is both available and more instructive.

Y = pca.transform(X_samples - X_samples.mean(axis=0))
print("variance explained by PC1..PC5:", np.round(pca.explained_variance_ratio_, 3))
for k in range(3):
    t, p = stats.ttest_ind(Y[status == 1, k], Y[status == 0, k])
    print("PC%d: diseased mean %+.2f, healthy %+.2f, t-test p = %.2e" % (k + 1, Y[status == 1, k].mean(),
                                                                         Y[status == 0, k].mean(), p))
print("correlation of PC1 with the library-size proxy: %.2f" % np.corrcoef(Y[:, 0], expr.sum(axis=0).to_numpy())[0, 1])

Figure 3. PC1 explains 27 % of the total variance and separates diseased from healthy sites (p = 4e-22 comparing PC1 scores between site types); PC2 explains 13 % and does not (p = 0.09). The thin lines join the two samples of the same patient: most are short, meaning the two sites of one patient resemble each other in the dimensions that PCA ranks highest - the structure that the paired analysis of the next section exploits.

Finding the design in the first principal component is reassuring but not automatic. In many data sets PC1 is the processing date, the RNA quality or the hospital, and the phenotype appears in PC4 if at all - the classic batch-effect situation[9] whose standard remedy, ComBat[10], also removes real signal when the batch is confounded with the condition. Here the only grouping variable the series provides is the patient, so the patient is what we model.

4. Differential expression with a paired linear model

For one gene, write the expression of sample $s$ as

$$y_s = \mu + \beta\,\text{diseased}_s + \alpha_{\text{patient}(s)} + \varepsilon_s,$$

a linear model with one coefficient of interest, $\beta$, and one intercept per patient. The patient terms absorb everything that makes a person's gingiva different from another's - genotype, age, oral hygiene, the unmeasured covariates this series does not provide - so $\beta$ is estimated from within-patient contrasts only. For a design with exactly two samples per patient this model is algebraically identical to a paired t-test on the differences, and the next cell demonstrates the identity rather than asserting it.

Worked example: one gene, by hand

Take TNFRSF17, a plasma-cell marker. For each of the 69 patients compute the difference diseased - healthy; the first five are +2.834, +3.582, +0.403, -0.191 and +2.935 log2 units. The mean of all 69 differences is 2.1312 and their standard deviation is 1.7268, so the standard error is 1.7268/sqrt(69) = 0.2079 and the paired t statistic is 2.1312/0.2079 = 10.25 with 68 degrees of freedom, giving p = 1.96e-15. The same number must come out of the linear model with 69 patient intercepts, and out of scipy.stats.ttest_rel. The unpaired test on the same gene gives t = 8.25 instead, because it must compete against the between-patient variability that the pairing removes.

gene = "TNFRSF17"
y = expr.loc[gene, cols].to_numpy(dtype=float)
d_vals = np.array([expr.loc[gene, p + "_D"] - expr.loc[gene, p + "_H"] for p in patients])
t_hand = d_vals.mean() / (d_vals.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(d_vals)))
print("by hand      : mean difference %.4f, sd %.4f, SE %.4f, t = %.3f, p = %.3e"
      % (d_vals.mean(), d_vals.std(ddof=1), d_vals.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(d_vals)), t_hand,
         2 * stats.t.sf(abs(t_hand), len(d_vals) - 1)))
print("scipy paired : t = %.3f, p = %.3e" % stats.ttest_rel(
    expr.loc[gene, [p + "_D" for p in patients]].to_numpy(dtype=float),
    expr.loc[gene, [p + "_H" for p in patients]].to_numpy(dtype=float)))

patient_dummies = pd.get_dummies(pd.Categorical([c[:4] for c in cols]), drop_first=True).to_numpy(dtype=float)
X_paired = sm.add_constant(np.column_stack([status.astype(float), patient_dummies]))
fit_paired = sm.OLS(y, X_paired).fit()
fit_simple = sm.OLS(y, sm.add_constant(status.astype(float).reshape(-1, 1))).fit()
print("statsmodels, patient terms   : beta = %.4f, t = %.3f, p = %.3e, residual df = %d"
      % (fit_paired.params[1], fit_paired.tvalues[1], fit_paired.pvalues[1], fit_paired.df_resid))
print("statsmodels, no patient term : beta = %.4f, t = %.3f, p = %.3e"
      % (fit_simple.params[1], fit_simple.tvalues[1], fit_simple.pvalues[1]))

Dmat = expr[[p + "_D" for p in patients]].to_numpy()
Hmat = expr[[p + "_H" for p in patients]].to_numpy()
delta = Dmat - Hmat                                   # genes x patients, within-patient log2 fold changes
log2fc = delta.mean(axis=1)
t_paired, p_paired = stats.ttest_rel(Dmat, Hmat, axis=1)
t_unpaired, p_unpaired = stats.ttest_ind(Dmat, Hmat, axis=1, equal_var=True)
q_paired = multipletests(p_paired, method="fdr_bh")[1]
q_unpaired = multipletests(p_unpaired, method="fdr_bh")[1]
res = pd.DataFrame({"log2FC": log2fc, "t": t_paired, "p": p_paired, "q": q_paired}, index=expr.index)
print("genes at FDR < 0.05 - paired: %d | unpaired: %d  (of %d tested)"
      % ((q_paired < 0.05).sum(), (q_unpaired < 0.05).sum(), len(res)))
print("paired p smaller than unpaired p for %d of %d genes" % ((p_paired < p_unpaired).sum(), len(res)))
print("adding an effect-size filter to the paired list: |log2FC| > 0.5 -> %d genes | > 1 -> %d genes"
      % (((q_paired < 0.05) & (np.abs(log2fc) > 0.5)).sum(), ((q_paired < 0.05) & (np.abs(log2fc) > 1)).sum()))
print("median |log2FC| among the FDR-significant genes: %.3f" % np.median(np.abs(log2fc[q_paired < 0.05])))
print("\nstrongest increases in diseased tissue:")
print(res.sort_values("log2FC", ascending=False).head(8).to_string(float_format=lambda v: "%.4g" % v))

Three numbers deserve comment. 3,766 of 5,000 genes reach FDR < 0.05 in the paired analysis and 3,420 in the unpaired one; the pairing buys about 350 extra discoveries and lowers the p-value for 92 % of genes, which is what a within-subject design is for. But a list of 3,766 "significant" genes out of 5,000 is not a result - it says that diseased and healthy gingiva differ almost everywhere, which is biologically true for an inflamed tissue invaded by plasma cells and useless as a shortlist. The median significant gene changes by 0.43 log2 units, a factor of 1.35. Adding an effect-size requirement is therefore not cosmetic: at |log2FC| > 1 (a two-fold change) the list falls to 204 genes, which a wet-lab collaborator can act on. Report both the statistical and the effect-size criterion, and say which genes the threshold removed.

Note also what the 5,000 genes are: the most variable genes of the original 54,675 probe sets, selected when the course data set was frozen. That pre-filter was applied blind to the diseased/healthy labels, so it does not inflate the comparison - but a filter chosen with the labels in view (for example "keep genes that differ between groups") would be the first form of double dipping, and section 8 returns to it.

5. Volcano, MA and heatmap, done properly

Three plots carry a differential-expression analysis into a paper, and each has a standard way of being misleading. The volcano plot (effect size against significance) invites reading significance as importance; drawing both thresholds on it, and annotating only genes that pass both, fixes that. The MA plot (effect against average abundance) exists to reveal intensity-dependent bias - a trend in the cloud means the normalisation failed. The heatmap is the most dangerous of the three: selecting the most significant genes and then showing that they separate the groups is circular, and the picture will look convincing even when built on noise. The honest heatmap either uses genes chosen independently of the comparison, or is labelled as an illustration of the selection rather than evidence for it.

6. Over-representation analysis, by hand

The gene list must now be turned into biology. The simplest method asks, for each gene set, whether the overlap with our list is larger than chance under a hypergeometric distribution: drawing $n$ genes (the list) without replacement from $N$ genes (the universe) of which $K$ belong to the set, the probability of seeing at least $k$ in common is

$$P(X \ge k) = \sum_{j=k}^{\min(n,K)} \frac{\binom{K}{j}\binom{N-K}{n-j}}{\binom{N}{n}}.$$

Two decisions matter more than the formula. The universe $N$ must be the genes that could have been detected - here the 5,000 genes in the matrix, not the 20,000 genes of the genome, or every p-value is wrong in the optimistic direction. And the list depends on the thresholds of section 4, so an over-representation result inherits every arbitrary choice made there.

def read_gmt(path, universe, min_size=10, max_size=500):
    sets = {}
    for line in open(path, encoding="utf-8"):
        fields = line.rstrip("\n").split("\t")
        members = set(fields[2:]) & universe
        if min_size <= len(members) <= max_size:
            sets[fields[0]] = members
    return sets

universe = set(expr.index)
kegg = read_gmt(data_path("genesets_kegg_2021.gmt"), universe)
gobp = read_gmt(data_path("genesets_gobp_2023.gmt"), universe)
up = set(expr.index[(q_paired < 0.05) & (log2fc > 0.5)])
down = set(expr.index[(q_paired < 0.05) & (log2fc < -0.5)])
print("gene sets kept (10-500 members inside the universe): KEGG %d, GO-BP %d" % (len(kegg), len(gobp)))
print("list sizes: %d up-regulated, %d down-regulated, universe %d" % (len(up), len(down), len(universe)))

def ora(selected, sets, N):
    rows = []
    for name, members in sets.items():
        k = len(selected & members)
        if k == 0:
            continue
        rows.append((name, len(members), k, len(selected) * len(members) / N,
                     hypergeom.sf(k - 1, N, len(members), len(selected))))
    out = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["set", "size", "overlap", "expected", "p"]).sort_values("p")
    out["q"] = multipletests(out["p"], method="fdr_bh")[1]
    return out.reset_index(drop=True)

ora_up, ora_down = ora(up, kegg, len(universe)), ora(down, kegg, len(universe))
print("\nKEGG sets at FDR < 0.05: %d for the up-regulated list, %d for the down-regulated one"
      % ((ora_up["q"] < 0.05).sum(), (ora_down["q"] < 0.05).sum()))
print(ora_up.head(8).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: "%.3g" % v))

The output is biologically coherent, which is the first thing to check: neutrophil extracellular trap formation, cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction, leukocyte transendothelial migration and B-cell activation are exactly what an inflamed, plasma-cell-rich gingival lesion should show[14]. Note two structural features of the output. Forty-four KEGG pathways are significant for the up-regulated list and none for the down-regulated one, and the GO-BP results contain large families of overlapping terms - "B cell activation", "B cell receptor signaling pathway", "antigen receptor-mediated signaling" share most of their genes. GO terms are a hierarchy, so their tests are far from independent and the significant list is highly redundant; reporting the top twenty terms is reporting one finding twenty times. Summarising by semantic clustering, or showing only the most specific term of each branch, is the standard remedy.

7. Gene-set enrichment analysis from its definition

Over-representation throws away two things: the ranking inside the list, and every gene that missed the threshold. A pathway in which a hundred genes all move slightly upwards may contain no gene at FDR < 0.05 and still be the most interesting result in the study. Gene-set enrichment analysis (GSEA)[6][7] was designed for that case. Rank all genes by a signed statistic, walk down the ranking, add to a running sum when a gene belongs to the set (weighted by the magnitude of its statistic) and subtract when it does not; the enrichment score is the maximum deviation of that walk from zero. Significance comes from a permutation null, and the score is normalised by the mean of the null values of the same sign to give the normalised enrichment score (NES), which can be compared across sets of different size.

Two permutation schemes exist and they are not equivalent. Permuting sample labels rebuilds the whole statistic and preserves the correlation between genes - this is the recommended scheme whenever the sample size allows it. Permuting gene labels is far cheaper but treats genes as exchangeable, which they are not, and is known to be anti-conservative for correlated sets[23][26]. We implement the gene-label version for speed and state the consequence, which is the honest way to use it.

order = np.argsort(-t_paired)
ranked_genes = expr.index.to_numpy()[order]
ranked_stat = t_paired[order]
weights = np.abs(ranked_stat)
position = {g: i for i, g in enumerate(ranked_genes)}

def enrichment_score(mask, w):
    '''Weighted Kolmogorov-Smirnov-like running sum; returns the maximum deviation from zero.'''
    hit = mask * w
    p_hit = np.cumsum(hit) / hit.sum()
    p_miss = np.cumsum(~mask) / (~mask).sum()
    dev = p_hit - p_miss
    return dev[np.argmax(np.abs(dev))], dev

rng_gsea = np.random.default_rng(0)
perms = [rng_gsea.permutation(len(ranked_genes)) for _ in range(200)]
rows = []
for name, members in kegg.items():
    idx = np.array([position[g] for g in members])
    mask = np.zeros(len(ranked_genes), bool); mask[idx] = True
    es, _ = enrichment_score(mask, weights)
    null = np.empty(len(perms))
    for i, pm in enumerate(perms):
        m2 = np.zeros(len(ranked_genes), bool); m2[pm[:len(idx)]] = True
        null[i] = enrichment_score(m2, weights)[0]
    same_side = null[null >= 0] if es >= 0 else null[null < 0]
    nes = es / np.abs(same_side).mean() if len(same_side) else np.nan
    pval = ((np.sum(same_side >= es) + 1) / (len(same_side) + 1) if es >= 0
            else (np.sum(same_side <= es) + 1) / (len(same_side) + 1))
    rows.append((name, len(idx), es, nes, pval))
gsea = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["set", "size", "ES", "NES", "p"]).sort_values("p")
gsea["q"] = multipletests(gsea["p"], method="fdr_bh")[1]
print("KEGG sets with GSEA q < 0.05: %d (%d with positive NES, %d negative)"
      % ((gsea["q"] < 0.05).sum(), ((gsea["q"] < 0.05) & (gsea["NES"] > 0)).sum(),
         ((gsea["q"] < 0.05) & (gsea["NES"] < 0)).sum()))
print(gsea.head(8).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: "%.4g" % v))

sets_ora = set(ora_up.loc[ora_up["q"] < 0.05, "set"])

merged = gsea.merge(ora_up[["set", "p"]], on="set", suffixes=("_gsea", "_ora"), how="inner")

      % (len(sets_ora), len(sets_gsea), len(sets_ora & sets_gsea)))

Figure 6. Top left: the running enrichment score for the strongest positively enriched KEGG pathway; the score climbs steeply because its genes (ticks, bottom left) are concentrated at the top of the ranking. Top right: GSEA normalised enrichment score against the over-representation p-value, set by set - the two agree in direction and broadly in strength. Bottom right: 42 of the 44 pathways found by over-representation are also found by GSEA, which additionally reports 25 that the threshold-based method missed, including apoptosis, antigen processing and presentation and ECM-receptor interaction.

The reconciliation rule is simple. Sets found by both are solid. Sets found only by GSEA are typically broad and moderately shifted - plausible but dependent on the permutation scheme, and with gene-label permutation their p-values are optimistic. Sets found only by over-representation are usually driven by a handful of very large fold changes, so they survive a threshold but not a whole-distribution test. Report the method, the gene-set database with its version, the universe, the permutation scheme and the number of permutations; without those five items an enrichment table cannot be reproduced[21][22].

Exercise 2

Rerun the GSEA block ranking genes by log2FC instead of by the t statistic. Which pathways change rank, and why does ranking by effect size alone promote noisy, low-expression genes? Then increase the number of permutations from 200 to 1,000 and check how much the smallest achievable p-value changes - the permutation count sets a floor of 1/(n+1) on it.

8. The four ways an omics analysis goes wrong

p much greater than n. Five thousand tests on 69 pairs: even under a perfect null, 250 genes would reach p < 0.05 by chance. The remedy - false-discovery-rate control[11][8] - is standard, but its validity depends on the p-values being correctly calibrated, which brings the next point.

The permutation scheme must respect the design. Shuffling the diseased/healthy labels across all 138 samples breaks the pairing and treats two samples from one patient as independent; the resulting null is wrong. Flipping the two labels within each patient is the correct paired permutation. The cell below runs both.

Double dipping. Choosing genes with the labels in view and then evaluating a classifier - or a heatmap, or a test - on the same samples is circular[12]. The demonstration below uses random labels, where the true accuracy is 0.5 by construction.

The winner's curse. The effect sizes of the genes selected for being the most extreme are biased upwards, so they shrink in an independent cohort[24][25]. Splitting the patients in two halves measures that shrinkage directly.

rng_p = np.random.default_rng(1)
y_wrong = rng_p.permutation(status)                      # permute across patients: breaks the pairing
Dw_ = expr.to_numpy()[:, y_wrong == 1]; Hw_ = expr.to_numpy()[:, y_wrong == 0]
p_wrong = stats.ttest_ind(Dw_, Hw_, axis=1, equal_var=True).pvalue
rng_f = np.random.default_rng(2)
flip = rng_f.integers(0, 2, len(patients)).astype(bool)   # correct paired permutation: swap within patient
p_right = stats.ttest_rel(np.where(flip[None, :], Hmat, Dmat), np.where(flip[None, :], Dmat, Hmat), axis=1).pvalue
print("null by permuting labels ACROSS patients : raw p < 0.05 for %d genes, FDR < 0.05 for %d"
      % ((p_wrong < 0.05).sum(), (multipletests(p_wrong, method="fdr_bh")[1] < 0.05).sum()))
print("null by flipping labels WITHIN patients  : raw p < 0.05 for %d genes, FDR < 0.05 for %d"
      % ((p_right < 0.05).sum(), (multipletests(p_right, method="fdr_bh")[1] < 0.05).sum()))
print("expected under a correct null            : about %d genes at raw p < 0.05" % int(0.05 * len(expr)))

null by permuting labels ACROSS patients : raw p < 0.05 for 1256 genes, FDR < 0.05 for 0
null by flipping labels WITHIN patients  : raw p < 0.05 for 69 genes, FDR < 0.05 for 0
expected under a correct null            : about 250 genes at raw p < 0.05

# Double dipping, measured on random labels where the truth is known to be 0.5
pair_cols = [c for p_ in patients for c in (p_ + "_D", p_ + "_H")]
rng_n = np.random.default_rng(3)
y_null = np.concatenate([[1, 0] if f else [0, 1] for f in rng_n.integers(0, 2, len(patients)).astype(bool)])
Xp = expr[pair_cols].to_numpy().T
groups_p = np.array([c[:4] for c in pair_cols], dtype=object)
X_leaky = SelectKBest(f_classif, k=50).fit_transform(Xp, y_null)          # selection sees ALL samples
acc_leaky = cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(max_iter=3000), X_leaky, y_null,
                            cv=GroupKFold(5), groups=groups_p).mean()
pipe = Pipeline([("select", SelectKBest(f_classif, k=50)), ("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=3000))])
acc_honest = cross_val_score(pipe, Xp, y_null, cv=GroupKFold(5), groups=groups_p).mean()
print("RANDOM labels (true accuracy 0.500):")
print("   gene selection outside the cross-validation : %.3f" % acc_leaky)
print("   gene selection inside each training fold    : %.3f" % acc_honest)

# Winner's curse: discover in half the patients, measure in the other half
rng_h = np.random.default_rng(0); perm = rng_h.permutation(len(patients))
half1 = [patients[i] for i in perm[:34]]; half2 = [patients[i] for i in perm[34:]]
def paired_stats(ps):
    Dd = expr[[p_ + "_D" for p_ in ps]].to_numpy(); Hh = expr[[p_ + "_H" for p_ in ps]].to_numpy()
    tt, pp_ = stats.ttest_rel(Dd, Hh, axis=1)
    return (Dd - Hh).mean(axis=1), tt, pp_
l1, t1, _ = paired_stats(half1); l2, t2, p2 = paired_stats(half2)
sel = np.argsort(-np.abs(t1))[:100]
print("\ntop 100 genes by |t| in the discovery half:")
print("   mean |log2FC| in the discovery half  : %.3f" % np.abs(l1[sel]).mean())
print("   mean |log2FC| in the validation half : %.3f (shrinkage %.0f %%)"
      % (np.abs(l2[sel]).mean(), 100 * (1 - np.abs(l2[sel]).mean() / np.abs(l1[sel]).mean())))
print("   replicating at p < 0.05 with the same sign: %d of 100" % int(((p2[sel] < 0.05) &
      (np.sign(l1[sel]) == np.sign(l2[sel]))).sum()))

Figure 7. Left: permuting the labels across patients leaves 1,256 genes at raw p < 0.05, five times the 250 expected, because two samples of one patient are correlated and the test treats them as independent; the correct within-patient flip leaves 69, and neither scheme produces a single FDR-significant gene. Centre: with labels assigned at random, selecting the fifty best genes before cross-validation gives 0.574 accuracy where the truth is 0.500, while selecting inside each fold gives 0.428 - noise around chance. Right: the hundred genes with the largest |t| in a random half of the patients lose 12 % of their apparent effect in the other half, with points systematically below the diagonal.

The winner's-curse panel also carries good news that should be stated, since this unit is otherwise a catalogue of traps: all 100 selected genes replicate at p < 0.05 with the same sign in the validation half. When an effect is large, widespread and measured in a paired design, omics results do replicate - the 12 % shrinkage is the honest correction to apply to the headline effect sizes, not a reason to distrust the finding. What the single cohort cannot deliver is generalisation: one population, one clinical protocol, one array platform, and - as the series metadata make explicit - no age, sex or smoking information with which to check that the comparison is not confounded by something the sampling happened to align with.

9. Summary

Omics analysis is ordinary statistics applied under three unusual conditions: thousands of variables, few and non-independent samples, and a result that is a list rather than a prediction. The sequence half of this unit made the non-independence visible in the 621 reviewed UniProt sequences: a nearest-neighbour family classifier on dipeptide profiles scored 0.947 under a random split and 0.879 once homologous sequences were kept in one fold, while logistic regression on the same features lost only 0.995 to 0.982 - and the diagnostic behind both numbers is that the random split leaves 22 % of test sequences a relative above 0.9 similarity in the training set, against 0 % after grouping. The rule that follows is to cluster first (345 homology groups here) and let the clusters be the groups of the cross-validator, reporting the grouped number as the performance of the method. The expression half used the frozen gingival-tissue matrix: 5,000 genes, 138 samples, 69 within-patient pairs, log2 RMA intensities with a library-size proxy varying by 2.2 % and no demographic covariates at all. PC1 carried 27 % of the variance and separated diseased from healthy sites; PC2 did not.

A paired linear model with one intercept per patient reproduced the paired t-test exactly (TNFRSF17: beta = 2.131, t = 10.25, p = 2e-15, against t = 8.25 unpaired), and over the whole matrix the pairing gave the smaller p-value for 92 % of genes and 3,766 discoveries at FDR < 0.05 against 3,420 unpaired. That number is also a warning: with three-quarters of the measured genes significant, statistical significance has stopped being a filter, and the effect-size criterion |log2FC| > 1 - which leaves 204 genes - is what makes the list actionable. Over-representation analysis implemented from the hypergeometric distribution found 44 KEGG pathways for the up-regulated list and none for the down-regulated one, led by neutrophil extracellular trap formation and cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction; a permutation GSEA written from its definition found 67 positive sets, 42 of them shared with over-representation, and the two were reconciled set by set rather than reported separately.

The closing experiments quantified the four classic failures. Permuting labels across patients instead of within them produced 1,256 false positives at raw p < 0.05 where 250 are expected. Selecting genes before cross-validation rather than inside it raised the accuracy on random labels from 0.428 to 0.574. The hundred strongest genes of a discovery half lost 12 % of their effect size in the validation half, although all hundred replicated in sign and significance. And the heatmap of the most differential genes - the figure most likely to appear in a thesis - is circular by construction and must be labelled as an illustration. Three habits are worth carrying into the group's periodontitis work: write down the universe, the thresholds and the permutation scheme before computing anything; make the patient, not the sample, the unit of analysis; and treat every list as provisional until it has been seen in a second cohort[9][12].

10. Self-assessment

1. Why is a random train/test split wrong for a protein-family classifier, and what replaces it?

Because homologous sequences are near-duplicates: a random split leaves a close relative of almost every test sequence in the training set, so the model can memorise rather than generalise. Cluster the sequences at an identity threshold (CD-HIT, MMseqs2 or the pre-computed UniRef clusters) and use those clusters as the groups of a group-aware cross-validator; the grouping variable can never be the class label itself. Here the nearest-neighbour model fell from 0.947 to 0.879 and 22 % of test sequences lost a near-identical relative from the training set.

2. These data are log2 RMA microarray intensities. Why not use DESeq2 or PyDESeq2?

Those methods model integer counts with a negative-binomial mean-variance relationship produced by sequencing. Microarray intensities are continuous and already normalised, so the count model does not apply. The right tool is a per-gene linear model with moderated variance (the limma family), which is what the paired model here implements.

3. What does the patient term in the linear model do, and what is the price of including it?

It absorbs every stable between-patient difference, so the treatment coefficient is estimated from within-patient contrasts only; this is why 92 % of genes get a smaller p-value. The price is degrees of freedom - 68 instead of 136 - and the inability to estimate any effect that does not vary within a patient, such as a patient-level covariate.

4. 3,766 of 5,000 genes are significant. Is that a good result?

It is a correct result and a useless list. With a tissue-wide inflammatory response the null is false nearly everywhere, so significance no longer discriminates. Add an effect-size threshold (204 genes at |log2FC| > 1), report the median effect size of the significant set (0.43 log2 units here), and move the interpretation to gene sets.

5. Why must the universe of an over-representation test be the measured genes rather than the genome?

Because the hypergeometric model asks how surprising the overlap is given what could have been drawn. Using 20,000 genes when only 5,000 could be selected inflates the apparent enrichment and shrinks every p-value. The universe, the list and the thresholds must all be reported.

6. What does GSEA see that over-representation cannot?

Coordinated, moderate shifts: a set whose genes all move slightly in the same direction without any single gene passing the threshold. GSEA uses the whole ranking and the magnitude of each statistic, so it needs no threshold at all. Here it recovered 42 of the 44 over-representation hits plus 25 further sets.

7. Gene-label and sample-label permutation give different GSEA p-values. Which is right?

Sample-label permutation, because it preserves the correlation structure between genes; gene-label permutation treats genes as exchangeable and is anti-conservative for correlated sets. Gene-label permutation is acceptable when the sample size is too small to permute, provided the choice is stated.

8. You permute the diseased/healthy labels of all 138 samples and still find 1,256 genes at raw p < 0.05. What went wrong?

The permutation broke the pairing: samples from the same patient are correlated, so a permutation that mixes them does not generate a valid null for a test that assumes independence. Flip the two labels within each patient instead, which respects the design and returns the expected behaviour.

9. A colleague selects the 50 most differential genes, trains a classifier with cross-validation and reports 92 % accuracy. What is the flaw and how is it fixed?

The selection used the labels of all samples, including those in each test fold, so information leaked. Put the selection inside the cross-validation pipeline so it is refitted on each training fold. On random labels, that distinction moved the accuracy from 0.574 to 0.428 in this data set.

10. What is the winner's curse and how large was it here?

Genes selected for having the most extreme statistics have effect sizes biased upwards by the selection, so they shrink in independent data. The hundred strongest genes of a discovery half of the patients lost 12 % of their mean |log2FC| in the validation half - while all hundred still replicated in sign and significance.

11. The series has no sex, age or smoking information. What can and cannot be claimed?

Within-patient comparisons remain valid, because each patient is their own control and every stable personal covariate cancels. What cannot be done is checking whether the diseased-site effect differs by sex or age, adjusting for smoking, or claiming that the cohort represents any wider population.

12. Which five items must accompany an enrichment table for it to be reproducible?

The method (ORA or GSEA, and which statistic was ranked), the gene-set database with its version and date, the universe of genes, the selection thresholds or the ranking metric, and the permutation scheme with the number of permutations. Multiple-testing correction and the software versions complete the list.

Glossary

FASTA
Plain-text format for sequences: a header line starting with ">" followed by the residues.
k-mer features
Counts or frequencies of all substrings of length k (here dipeptides, 400 of them) used as a fixed-length numeric representation of a sequence.
Group split
Cross-validation in which all members of a group (homology cluster, patient, scaffold) stay in the same fold.
Orthologue / paralogue
The same protein in two species / two copies within one genome; both are homologues and both make two rows of a sequence table statistically dependent.
log2 RMA intensity
Robust multi-array average summary of a microarray probe set on a log2 scale; a difference of 1 is a two-fold change.
Paired design
Two measurements from the same unit (here the diseased and healthy site of one patient), analysed through their difference.
log2 fold change
Mean within-patient difference on the log2 scale; the effect size of a differential-expression analysis.
Benjamini-Hochberg FDR
Procedure keeping all genes whose sorted p-value is below 0.05k/m, controlling the expected proportion of false discoveries among those declared.
Volcano plot
Effect size against -log10 p; both thresholds must be drawn for it to be read correctly.
MA plot
Effect size against average intensity; a trend indicates a normalisation problem.
Over-representation analysis (ORA)
Hypergeometric test of the overlap between a selected gene list and a gene set, relative to a declared universe.
Gene-set enrichment analysis (GSEA)
Threshold-free test using the whole ranking; the enrichment score is the maximum deviation of a weighted running sum.
Normalised enrichment score (NES)
Enrichment score divided by the mean of the same-sign permutation scores, comparable across set sizes.
Double dipping / circular analysis
Using the same data to select features and to evaluate them, which inflates every subsequent statistic.
Winner's curse
Upward bias of the effect sizes of the items selected for being most extreme; measured by replication in held-out samples.
Batch effect
Technical variation associated with processing groups; dangerous when confounded with the condition of interest.

Textbooks

  • Hastie T, Tibshirani R, Friedman J. The Elements of Statistical Learning. 2nd ed. Springer; 2009. - Chapter 18 on the p >> n problem and on multiple testing.
  • Holmes S, Huber W. Modern Statistics for Modern Biology. Cambridge University Press; 2019. - High-throughput count data, testing and multiple comparisons, freely available online.
  • Wasserman L. All of Statistics. Springer; 2004. - Chapters 10 and 15 for the testing background.
  • VanderPlas J. Python Data Science Handbook. 2nd ed. O'Reilly; 2022. - pandas and matplotlib idioms used here.

Online resources

  • Biopython tutorial and cookbook: biopython.org/docs/latest/Tutorial.
  • UniProt, the source of the frozen family set, and its UniRef clustered views: uniprot.org.
  • Bioconductor workflows for RNA-seq and microarray analysis: bioconductor.org workflows.
  • GSEA and MSigDB documentation: gsea-msigdb.org.
  • Enrichr gene-set libraries (the source of the frozen GMT files): maayanlab.cloud/Enrichr.
  • NCBI GEO, where the series analysed here is archived: ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo.
